*letzte*de{}|Etymology}From Middle High German lest,a contraction of from Middle High German lezzest,from Old High German lezzist (also from Old High German lazzōst),itself superlative of from Old High German laz (cognate to from English late). The modern German form with ''-tz-'' is of northern origin; two separate origins have probably met in it:Firstly,there is a general tendency in some Central German dialects of inserting ''-t-'' before comparative and superlative endings. (Compare for this,for example,Ripuarian from Central Franconian fröh → from Central Franconian fröhter,from Central Franconian fröhtste). Secondly,from Middle Low German lest,contracted superlative of from Middle Low German late,had a regular or regularized variant from Middle Low German letst,which is very rare in writing,but may have been more common in spoken dialects. (Compare modern from German Low German lättst.) Related forms are from Dutch laatst and from Dutch lest,from English latest and from English last,from Luxembourgish lescht,from Hunsrik letst.|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈlɛt͡stə/}Ⓓd/db/De-letzte.ogg}letz+te|Adjective}#last}•Das war der '''letzte''' Zug.}•That was the last train.}•Er hat seine '''letzte''' Freundin betrogen.}•He cheated on his last girlfriend.}#}letzte Vielleicht träume ich? *Leutnant*de{}wikipedia:langde|Alternative forms}Leutenant}Lieutenant|Etymology}From Middle French lieutenant; deputy,from French tenir from French le from French lieu from French de (“to keep the position of”). Early on,the form was folk-etymologically reshaped,the first syllable being associated with Leute,the last syllable sometimes with Amt. The normal spoken form in German has been ''Leut(e)nant'' since the 17th century,although the French spelling ''Lieutenant'' remained common and became standard in the 19th century. The contemporary spelling was introduced in the German Empire in 1899 amid rising Franco-German tensions and a general trend of Germanification.|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈlɔʏ̯tnant/}Ⓓa/a7/De-Leutnant.ogg}Leut+nant}Rhymes:ant|Noun}(mask.,plural:[Leutnantes])}#lieutenant|Usage notes}The normal plural used to be ''Leutnants''. Today both forms are roughly equally common. The preference seems to depend somewhat on stress patterns,meaning that  is more frequent in the simplex than in compounds.|Derived terms}Generalleutnant}Kapitänleutnant}Leutnantspatent}Oberleutnant

*lieben*de{}|Etymology 1}from Proto-Indo-European idlove}Formally from Middle High German lieben,alteration (based on from Middle High German liep) of rarer from Middle High German tto make or be dear,to treat in a friendly way,from Old High German liuben,equivalent to lieb+en.}The singularly attested from Old High German tto love probably remained without continuation; the modern sense was derived in late Middle High German from the noun liebe on the model of from Middle High German tto love,from Middle High German minne,which had developed a sexual overtone. It remained absent from most traditional dialects,which use variants of lieb haben or gern haben instead (compare the usage note below). Related to from English love. Compare from Dutch lieven.|Pronunciation}IPA:ˈliːbm̩}De-lieben2.ogg}De-lieben.ogg}lie+ben}liebem some speakers}Rhymes:iːbən|Verb}de-verb}#usually to love,to have a strong affection for (someone or something)}•Ich '''liebe''' dich.}•I '''love''' you.}•Ich '''liebe''' die französische Sprache.}•I '''love''' the French language.}#reflexive to love one another}#reflexive to make love,to have sex|Usage notes}German is more reluctant in its use of ''lieben'' (“to love”) than is English,particularly in reference to things. Such phrases as “''Ich liebe den Teppich in deinem Zimmer!''” (“I love the carpet in your room!”) are a typical feature of “dubbing German”,i.e. literal translations from English as commonly found in dubbed films or sitcoms. A more native way of expressing the same in German would be “''Der Teppich in deinem Zimmer sieht toll aus!''”,or “''Der Teppich in deinem Zimmer gefällt mir sehr gut!''”,or something along these lines.}Even when referring to love between people,''lieben'' may have a slightly solemn sound. A more normal way of expressing it in spoken German is lieb haben,particularly among friends and family,but usually also between lovers. (See the latter lemma for more.)|Adjective}lieben

*liefern*de{}|Etymology}From Middle High German lieveren (before 1350),which may be borrowed directly from Old French livrer,from Latin līberō,but was probably introduced via from Middle Dutch - and from Middle Low German lēveren (the vocalism ''-ie-'' then being due to hypercorrection; compare also attested ''liebern''). Low German definitely contributed to the spread of the word,which was part of the technical vocabulary of the Hanseatic League. Compare with modern from Dutch leveren,from Swedish leverera and from French livrer.|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈliːfɐn/}Ⓓe/ee/De-liefern.ogg}lie+fern|Verb}de-verb}#transitive to supply,provide liefern ( with  accgoods etc.+:an(acc)to someone/somewhere)}#transitive to deliver (goods,an order,etc.)}#}liefern Wichtiger ist,dass die Ware innerhalb einer definierten Zeit und an einen genau bestimmten Ort '''geliefert''' wird.}•More importantly,the goods are delivered in a specified time and place.}#transitive to yield gl:to produce an outcome of crops}#transitive to research,to read up on (information)}#reflexive to fight (a battle,a duel,a war)|Derived terms}abliefern}anliefern}ausliefern}beliefern}einliefern}energieliefernd}lieferbar}mitliefern}nachliefern}überliefern}zuliefern}Lieferant}Lieferengpass}Lieferschein}Lieferservice}Lieferung}Lieferwagen}Lieferzeit

*Lieschen*de{}|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈliːsçən/}Ⓓ3/3e/De-Lieschen.ogg|Proper noun}f:n,s,plural:[Lieschens])}#Given Name ''derived from'' Elisabeth}#primarily A generic name for a small railway or tramway.}#}Lieschen Folge dieser Wandlungen ist die Einstellung des Eisenbahnverkehrs auf der Privatbahnstrecke Reinheim-Reichelsheim (das Odenwald-"'''Lieschen'''") im Jahre 1963.}•The consequence of this transformation is the closure of rail transport on the private railway Reinheim-Reichelsheim (the Odenwald-"'''Lieschen'''") in 1963.}#}Lieschen Andere lokale Volksfeste machen dem Wäldchestag kräftig Konkurrenz,obgleich noch immer das »'''Lieschen'''« an diesem Tag zum Oberforsthaus hinausfährt,der Sonderzug der Straßenbahn}•Other local festivals are a strong competition to the Wäldschetag,although the "'''Lieschen'''" still runs on this day to the Oberforsthaus – the special train of the tramway.}#}Lieschen Das „Stockheimer '''Lieschen'''“ ist Kult. Auf Facebook hat die Strecke zwischen Glauburg-Stockheim und Bad Vilbel,die offiziell Niddertalbahn heißt,eine eigene Gruppe,auf der sich auch Mitfahrer aus Nidderau,Schöneck und Niederdorfelden austauschen.}•The "Stockheimer '''Lieschen'''" is cult. The railway between Glauburg-Stockheim and Bad Vilbel,officially called the Niddertalbahn,has a Facebook group where even riders from Nidderau,Schöneck and Niederdorfelden chat.|Usage notes}Like other female names in -chen,this is mostly construed as feminine () if the person is widely known under this name,but as neuter () if it is merely an occasional pet name. This,obviously,with the exclusion of those areas of western Germany where all female names may be treated as neuter.

*Maar*de{}|Alternative forms}obsolete|Etymology}Attested since at least the 16th century,from an underlying from Middle High German ⋆mar(e). Adopted into scientific parlance during the 19th century from gmw-cfr dialects of the Eifel region,home to many maars,which often include the word in their names. The Central Franconian term also has the broader sense of “pool,cesspit,swamp”,which touches on from Middle High German tbog or is even merged with it (cf. from Luxembourgish Muer and from Luxembourgish Mouer). Further origin uncertain,but surely related with the root of Meer and Moor. *Machtergreifung*de{}|Etymology}Macht (power)+Ergreifung (seizure) ,(from ergreifen+-ung (resultative verbal noun)),19th century.|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈmaχtʔɛɐ̯ˌɡʁaɪ̯fʊŋ/}Ⓓ2/25/De-Machtergreifung.ogg}Macht+er+grei+fung}Rhymes:aɪfʊŋ|Noun}(fem.)}#historical seizure of power,specifically in reference to Hitler's appointment as chancellor on 30 January 1933}•synononym [Machtübernahme],[Machtübertragung]}#}'''1858''',''Allgemeine österreichische Zeitung'',cited in ''Schwäbischer Merkur'' 13 October 1858,https://books.google.ch/books?idUiJNAAAAcAAJ&pgRA29-PP1#vonepage&q&ffalse 1093}#}:Das Vertrauen,mit dem ihm seine Unterthanen entgegenkommen,ist ein unbegrenztes,und die Befriedigung über seine '''Machtergreifung''' ist eine fast ausnahmslose.+tThe confidence which is extended to him i.e. the Prince Regent :w:William I,German Emperor+William of Hohenzollern   by his subjects is unlimited,and the gratification felt at his '''taking over the reins of power''' is all but universal.}#}Machtergreifung ... der pseudolegal verbrämte Prozeß der '''Machtergreifung''' und die Durchlöcherung der Weimarer Verfassung in den ersten Monaten des "Dritten Reiches" ...}•... the pseudo-legally embellished process of the '''seizure of power''' and the hollowing out of the Weimar constitution during the early months of the 'Third Reich' ...}#}Machtergreifung Trotzki,Sinowjew und Kamenew erleichterten Stalins '''Machtergreifung''',denn keiner von ihnen sah in ihm einen Rivalen für die Erbfolge.}•Trotsky,Zinovyev and Kamenev facilitated Stalin's '''seizure of power''',as none of them saw him as a rival in the order of succession.|Usage notes}Since the 1970s the terms Machtübertragung "transfer of power","transition of power" or Machtübernahme "acquisition of power" have been more commonly used as the unmarked terms for the (peaceful) transition of political power,as Machtergreifung has become strongly associated with 20th-century totalitarianism.

*Mama*de{}|Alternative forms}Mamma|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈmama/qualifier:commonly}IPA:/maˈmaː/qualifier:obsolete,lofty}Ⓓa/af/De-Mama.ogg}Rhymes:aː|Noun}(fem.,plural:[Mamas.gensprenominally without an article])}#mum,mummy,mom,mommy}•synononym Mutti|Usage notes}The word is commonly used with a definite article in most parts of central Germany,southern Germany,and Austria:''Wo ist die Mama?'' – “Where is Mum?” In northern Germany—and generally in writing—no article tends to be used:''Wo ist Mama?''}The genitive ''Mamas'' is used before the modified term,without any article or determiner:''Mamas Tasche'' – “Mum’s bag”. This is chiefly northern German usage; the rest of the language prefers:''die Tasche von der Mama'' (as above). — With an accompanying article or determiner,the genitive takes no ending:''die Tasche meiner Mama'' – “my mum’s bag”. This,however,is not common usage in any region; children will say instead:''die Tasche von meiner Mama.''|Derived terms}Mami qualifier:affectionate

*manch*de{}|Etymology}From Middle High German manec,from Old High German manag. The ''-ch'' is due to the traditional fricative pronunciation of non-initial ''-g-'' in Central German dialects. The spelling became predominant in Early New High German,possibly reinforced by the similar clusters in welch and solch. The original form has remained in mannigfach,manniglich,mannigfaltig,etc. Cognate with from Dutch menig,from English many,from Polish mnogi.|Pronunciation}IPA:-ntç}Ⓓ2/2d/De-manch.ogg|Pronoun}manch:}#used as an adjective or a noun many a; many; some|Usage notes}Only the inflected forms are commonly used in colloquial and informal German.}The bare form is sometimes used with a following adjective in literary German:''manch schöner Tag'' instead of ''mancher schöne Tag'' – “many a beautiful day”. Beiträge zur Buddhismuskunde und zur zentralasiatischen Märchenforschung'',Harrasowitz Verlag,Wiesbaden,p. 25 and 29:}#}:Da er ihn nicht in der Sonne aber auch nicht im Schatten bringen lassen sollte,befahl er dem '''Manne''',den Topf an die Spitze eines Stockes zu binden und mit einem dünnen Gewande zu bedecken.}#}:Dem '''Manne''' aber sagte er:...}#husband}•synononym [[[[[Ehemann],[Gatte]],[Ehegatte]],[Gemahl]],[Gespons g]],[m]}•Frau|Gesponsin|Ehegesponsin}•Ehepartner|Usage notes}The normal plural is '''''Männer''''',which can be used in all contexts and is now used exclusively in contexts other than the following.}The unchanged plural ''Mann'' (inherited from Old and Middle High German) is sometimes used after numerals. It means "men" as a measure for size or strength of a group rather than individuals:''Mit drei Mann können wir den Schrank heben'' – "With three people we can lift the cupboard." Military or police personnel,team members,demonstrators and the like are often counted using this unchanged plural. This may actually include women.}The plural ''Mannen'' is now rare and somewhat poetic. It usually means a group of men,often soldiers,under the command or leadership of someone:''Cäsars Mannen'' ("Caesar's men"). It is sometimes heard in sports jargon:''die Mannen von Trainer XY'' ("coach XY's men").|Antonyms}antsense:man (male human),by gender Frau,Männin}antsense:man (male human),by age Junge,Knabe,Bube,Bub chiefly Swiss and Austrian|Hyponyms}Ackermann}Ampelmann}Amtmann}Arbeitsmann}Barmann}Bergmann}Blödmann}Bootsmann}Buhmann}Dönermann}Edelmann}Ehemann}Eismann}Englischmann}Ersatzmann}Exmann}Fährmann}Flachmann}FBI-Mann}Feuerwehrmann}Franzmann}Froschmann}Gefolgsmann}Geschäftsmann}Hampelmann}Hauptmann}Hausmann}Hengstmann}Hintermann}Jungmann}Kameramann}Kaufmann}Klostermann}Landmann}Landsmann}Lebemann}Mann im Mond}Milchmann}Müllmann}Mustermann}Nebenmann}Neumann}Nordmann}Obmann}Ostmann}Putzmann}Sämann}Sandmann}Saubermann}Schulmann}Schutzmann}Seemann}Sensenmann}Staatsmann}Strohmann}Supermann}Tochtermann}Tormann}Traummann}V-Mann}Vordermann}Wachmann}Wahlmann}Waidmann}Wandersmann}Wassermann}Weidmann}Wehrmann}Weihnachtsmann|Derived terms}bemannt}Butzemann}entmannen}ermannen}Flattermann}mannbar}Männchen}Männerbund}mannhaft}Mannheit}männiglich}Männin}Mannschaft}mannshoch}mannstoll}männlich}Mannomann}Mannmonat}Manntag}Pipimann}Pullermann}Schneemann}seinen Mann stehen}von Mann zu Mann}German Low German|Etymology}From Middle Low German man,from Old Saxon mann,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆mann,from Proto-Germanic ⋆mann-,from Proto-Indo-European ⋆mon-. *Maß*de{}|Alternative forms}de-CH-alt}Maas}Masz|Etymology}From Middle High German māz,from Old High German māza,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆mātu. Compare from Dutch size,measure,from Mato measure,amount,limit. More at from English mete.}Unrelated to Masse.|Pronunciation}IPA:/maːs/}Ⓓf/f2/De-Ma%C3%9F.ogg}Rhymes:aːs}Maas|Noun}(neut.)}#size}#extent}#measure (standard against which something can be judged)}•Ehrlichkeit ist das wahre '''Maß''' eines Mannes.}•Honesty is the true '''measure''' of a man.}#}'''1932''',Erich Mühsam,''Die Befreiung der Gesellschaft vom Staat'',in:Erich Mühsam:Prosaschriften II,Verlag europäische ideen Berlin (1978),page 260:}#}:Der Individualismus will umgekehrt den ungekürzten Lebensraum des Individuums zum '''Maß''' der gesellschaftlichen Daseinsform machen,ohne Rücksicht auf Gleichheit und Gesamtnutzen.+Individualism,in contrast,wants to make the unshortened living space of the individual the measure of the social form of being,without consideration for equality or total utility.|Usage notes}Most native speakers and even some dictionaries,for example https://www.dwds.de/wb/Ma%C3%9F#1 dwds.de,confuse this word ('''das Maß''') with the rare word ''die Maße'' (plural in all cases:Maßen),which is so archaic that it is only used in idiomatic expressions such as these:}in Maßen/mit Maßen (for example ''in '''Maßen''' trinken'' – "to drink in '''moderation'''")}ohne Maßen (archaic:sonder Maßen)}über alle Maßen/über die Maßen}In speaking,native speakers nevertheless normally use these idiomatic expressions grammatically correctly with the plural ''Maßen''. But when thinking about these expressions and especially while writing,native speakers sometimes use the incorrect form ''Maße'' because they think these idiomatic expressions use the word ''das Maß'',whose accusative plural is ''die Maße'' (when in fact these expressions use the word ''die Maße'',whose accusative plural is ''die Maßen''). Such was the case in the German Wiktionary until November 2021.}The professionally edited dictionary dwds.de presents these expressions grammatically correctly but does so confusingly without explanation or warning in the entry for ''das Maß''. It neither explains why most of these expressions use the form ''Maßen'' in the accusative plural nor explains that this is the accusative plural of ''die Maße''. (Expressions with ''mit'' of course use the dative plural,which is the same for both the familiar word ''das Maß'' and the rare word ''die Maße''.)|Hyponyms}Ausmaß}Bogenmaß}Ebenmaß}Entfernungsmaß}Flächenmaß}Flüssigkeitsmaß}Gewichtsmaß}Gleichmaß}Gurtmaß}Handelsmaß}Hohlmaß}Holzmaß}Litermaß}Längsmaß}Quermaß}Raummaß}Trockenmaß}Volumenmaß}Versmaß}Winkelmaß}Zuverlässigkeitsmaß|Derived terms}-mäßig}mäßigen}maßgeblich}maßhaltig}mäßig}maßlos}maßstäbig}maßstäblich|Noun}(fem.,plural:[Maßen])}#South Germany a litre/tankard of beer}#}Maß Rund 230 Schaustellerbetriebe,Gastronomen und Marktkaufleute waren auf dem Wasen dabei. Gestiegene Energie- und Nebenkosten wirkten sich aus:So kostete die '''Maß''' im Grandls Hofbräu Zelt 13,20 Euro - 60 Cent mehr als beim letzten Mal.}:translationAround 230 showmen,restauranteurs,and vendors were there at Oktoberfest. *meist-*de{}|Etymology}From meist.|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈmaɪ̯st-/|Prefix}meist-:}#forms the superlative of past participles when this form is used to express frequency}•das '''meist'''gelesene Buch}•the '''most''' read book}•footer{{q}•read most often,by most people}•der '''meist'''kritisierte Politiker}•the '''most''' criticized politician}•footer{{q}•criticized most often,by most people|Usage notes}Past participle superlatives that express a degree can be formed in the normal way,that is with the suffix -st:''die zerstörteste Stadt'' (“the most destroyed city”). Alternatively,''am meisten'' can be used before the positive form:''die am meisten zerstörte Stadt''. (The latter is only possible with participles.)}There may be a semantic difference between a superlative with ''meist-'' and a normal superlative (though this is not the case with every past participle and generally is not often relevant in practice). *meistenteils*de{}|Etymology}[meist]+[Teil].|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈmaɪ̯stəntaɪ̯ls/|Adverb}#mostly,to the most part}•synononym größtenteils}#}meistenteils Spät am Abend liessen wir uns über den See nach St. Sebastian übersetzen. Es sind immer Mädchen,welche hier die Stelle der:translationRuderer vertreten; sie umringen den Fremden,so wie er sich nur dem Wasser nähert,und eifern in unverständlichem Vaskisch mit einander um die Ehre in überzufahren. *melken*de{}|Etymology 1}From Middle High German mëlken,from Old High German melchan,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆melkan,from Proto-Germanic ⋆melkaną,from Proto-Indo-European ⋆h₂melǵ-.}The consonantism ''-lk-'' is regular High German. The difference between melken and Milch is due to the fact that the latter used to have a short vowel after ''-l-'' (Old High German from Old High German miluh). Compare from Dutch melken,from English milk,from Danish malke,from Norwegian mjølke.|Pronunciation}IPA:ˈmɛlkŋ̩}Ⓓ9/9d/De-melken.ogg}Ⓓ1/13/De-melken2.ogg}Ⓓc/c1/De-melken3.ogg}mel+ken|Verb}melken(milkt:melkt#molk:melkte,gemolken:gemelktrare,mölke:melkte)}#transitive to milk (a cow,goat etc.)}#transitive to drain; to draw from (someone or something),especially without consent; to milk (someone) for money,information,etc.|Usage notes}''Melken'' has full sets of both strong and weak forms,both being accepted as standard. The past participle ''gemolken'' is considerably more common than ''gemelkt''. *mir*Alemannic German|Etymology}From from Isthmus Mixe we.|Pronunciation}IPA:/mir/(i:stressed IPA:/mɪːr/; i:unstressed IPA:/mər/)|Pronoun}mir:}#personal we}#personal Form of [ich]:(to) me}German|Pronunciation}qualifier:standard IPA:/miːɐ̯/}:}Ⓓd/d1/De-mir.ogg}:}Ⓓa/a3/De-mir2.ogg}:}Rhymes:iːɐ̯}qualifier:colloquially in unstressed position IPA:/mə/|Etymology 1}From Isthmus Mixe me,from Isthmus Mixe me,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆miʀ,from Proto-Germanic me,from Proto-Indo-European ⋆(e)me-,from Proto-Indo-European me. Cognate with from Old English me. More at me,(English).|Pronoun}mir:}#personal Form of [ich]:me,to me:}•Er gab es '''mir'''.}•He gave it '''to me'''.}•'''Mir''' ist kalt.|Derived terms}mirs|Etymology 2}From Isthmus Mixe twe. The form originated through assimilation of from Middle High German wir with a preceding verb form and subsequent unetymological segmentation. This is possibly already an from Old High German - development,since a common Old High German ending of the 1st person plural was ''-em'',thus ''bittēm wir'' → ''}bittē-mir'' (modern bitten wir). The contraction as such is definitely old,though the common form of assimilation,both in written Old High German and written Middle High German,is through loss of the nasal:''bittē wir''. The form with ''mir'' may either be a younger development in Middle High German,or a more colloquial form that only later appeared in writing. Older age is suggested by the great dominance of ''mir'' throughout modern dialects of High German. Compare from Yiddish מיר,from Luxembourgish mir. Compare also from Southern Puebla Mixtec twe two,from Norwegian Nynorsk twe.|Pronoun}mir:}#dialectal wir}#}'''16th century/1874''',''Alsfelder Passionsspiel mit Wörterbuch herausgegeben von C. W. M. Grein'',p. 13 l. 458f. note:the text also has ''mer'' for 1st person plural nominative:}#}:'''Mir''' willen widder in die helle, Die armen sele siden und quellen.|Usage notes}The form is not common in those parts of northern Germany where Low German dialects have traditionally been spoken.}German Low German|Alternative forms}meer}mehr|Pronunciation}IPA:aaMecklenburg,Pomerania}IPA:aaHolstein,Lower Saxony,northern Brandenburg}IPA:aasouthern Brandenburg|Adjective}mir:}#Mecklenburg comparative of [vęl]; more}Middle High German|Etymology}From from Isthmus Mixe me,from from Proto-West Germanic ⋆miʀ,from from Proto-Germanic me,from from Proto-Indo-European ⋆(e)me-,m:me. *misslingen*de{}|Alternative forms}mißlingen|Etymology}from Middle High German misselingen,from Old High German missilingan|Pronunciation}IPA:mɪsˈlɪŋŋ̩}Ⓓe/e9/De-misslingen.ogg}miss+lin+gen}Rhymes:ɪŋn̩|Verb}misslingen(misslang,misslungen,misslänge,auxiliary:sein)}#intransitive to fail; to be unsuccessful}•synononym missglücken}•Antonym:gelingen}•Das ist dir aber gründlich '''misslungen'''!}•That was thoroughly unsuccessful for you!|Usage notes}Before 1996,this word and its various forms were spelled with an ß,i.e. mißlingen,mißlingt,mißlang,mißlungen... Since the German Spelling Reform of 1996,this word and its various forms are spelled with  instead.}The verb misslingen is rarely used with a human subject,so it rarely appears in the first-person or second-person forms. To indicate failure related to a person,the dative case is used,as illustrated in the example above.|Derived terms}Misslingen

*Mistwetter*de{}|Etymology}Technically a compound of [[[Mist]+[Wetter]]+[t1dung]]+[t2weather]. ''Mist!'' is a rather common interjection equivalent to from English crap. However,the word is not freely prefixed to nouns,which makes it seem likely that ''Mistwetter'' is originally "misty weather",pertaining to from Middle Low German mist. *mitteldeutsch*de{}|Etymology}From mittel-+deutsch.|Pronunciation}Ⓓ0/00/De-mitteldeutsch.ogg|Adjective}#relational Central German gl:from or pertaining to any area that is currently or was historically central Germany,or from or pertaining to the people,culture or dialects of this area}#}'''1979''',Klaus-Jürgen Fiacre,''Historische Lautlehre des Dialektes von Bévercé (Kanton Malmedy,Belgien)'' (series:''Romania occidentalis'',vol. I),p. 23:}#}:Die deutsche Sprach- und Mundartgruppe in Neu-Belgien wohnt in den Kantonen Eupen,St. Vith und Malmedy. ... Im Nordosten,in den Gemeinden Raeren,Hauset und Eynatten ( im Kanton Eupen ) spricht man das Ripuarisch-Fränkische,das stark von dem Sprachausdruck von Aachen beeinflusst ist und sich zweifellos dem Deutschen nähert. *moin*de{}|Alternative forms}Moin}Moin,Moin (might be perceived as foreign or artificial in some regions,e.g. Mecklenburg-Vorpommern)|Etymology}From,or from the same source as,from German Low German moin,beyond which the etymology is from German not clear; see that entry for more.|Pronunciation}IPA:/mɔɪn/}Ⓓ4/4a/De-moin.ogg}Ⓓ3/3f/De-moin2.ogg}Rhymes:ɔːɪn|Interjection}moin:}#colloquial hi|Usage notes}Increasingly used outside of Northern Germany.}German Low German|Etymology}from German Low German The etymology is not clear.}It stems possibly from moi,from German Low German gml,thus meaning would be '(have a) good one'. This would explain the pronunciation with/ŋ/in some areas,which would stem from regular inflection of from Low German moi.}It is also possible that this word is a borrowing from a from German Low German gmw-fri language,which would explain the vowel sequence/ɔːɪ/,which does not naturally occur in almost any Low German dialect.}Further,many sources say that the word comes from the Berlin area,representing the local pronunciation of from German morning:mɔɐ̯jɘn. The pronunciation would come either from local Low German (where the word was pronounced mɔrʝɘn) and then have undergone r-vocalisation,or from early modern Upper Saxonian (/mɔˤjən/or something similar),which is the German dialect that initially replaced Low German in Berlin. The word was understood as 'moin' by the rhotic dialects surrounding the city and spread north from them.}Should this word be a from West Frisian - or Berlinian borrowing,it is likely that it was later conflated with the Low German word ''moi'' (/moːɪ/).}A descent,at least partially,from a lost from German Low German - dialect has also been hypothesized.|Pronunciation}IPA:/mɔːɪn/}IPA:/mɔːɪŋ/|Interjection}moin:}#informal hi

*Mord*de{}|Etymology}From Middle High German mort,from Old High German mord,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆morþ,from Proto-Germanic ⋆murþą. Cognate with from Dutch moord,from English murth,from Swedish mord,from Finnish murha. Also related with from English murder,from French meurtre.|Pronunciation}IPA:mɔːt}Ⓓ6/66/De-Mord.ogg}Mord|Noun}(mask.,plural:[Mord(e)s])}#murder}#}Mord Der '''Mord''' ist,wie jedem gebildeten Staatsanwalt bekannt,eine Tat,die in der äußersten Ekstase und mit der kältesten Roheit begangen wird.}•Murder is,as known to every educated prosecutor,an act that is committed in utmost ecstasy and with the coldest brutality.|Usage notes}Certain milder cases of murder,such as the American second-degree murder,are often covered by Totschlag in German legal terminology and do not then qualify as ''Mord.''}An English phrase like “''Peter's murder''” is ambiguous as it can mean either “the murder that Peter committed” or “the murder by which Peter was killed”. In German,„''Peters Mord''” can only mean the former. The latter is expressed as „''der Mord '''an''' Peter''“ or by using the word Ermordung („''Peters Ermordung''”).|Derived terms}Achtfachmord}Auftragsmord}Bilanzselbstmord}Brudermord}Chinesenmord}Deutschenmord}Doppelmord}Doppelselbstmord}Drachenmord}Dreifachmord}Ehrenmord}Eifersuchtsmord}Elffachmord}Elternmord}Familienmord}Fememord}Feuermord}Foltermord}Freundesmord}Fünffachmord}Fötusmord}Foetusmord}Gattenmord}Geschwistermord}Giftmord}Gottesmord}Haustiermord}Heidenmord}Indianermord}Judenmord}Justizmord}Kindermord}Kindesmord}Kindsmord}Königsmord}Lustmord}Lynchmord}Massenmord}Massenselbstmord}Mehrfachmord}Menschenmord}Meuchelmord}Mitnahmeselbstmord}Mittsommermord}Mord und Totschlag}Muttermord}Nachahmungsselbstmord}Neunfachmord}Onkelmord}Polizistenmord}Quantenselbstmord}Raubmord}Ritualmord}Rufmord}Russenmord}Schwestermord}Sechsfachmord}Selbstmord}Serienmord}Sexualmord}Siebenfachmord}Tantenmord}Tyrannenmord}Vatermord}Vierfachmord}Völkermord}Zehnfachmord}Zweifachmord}Zwölffachmord|See also}Mordio,mordio

*muffig*de{}|Etymology}The senses "smelly" and "grumpy" go back to different origins. The former pertains to Muff from Middle Low German muffen; the latter to Muffel,which is an Upper German dialect word of unknown origin. In contemporary German both senses often overlap (see below). It is therefore impossible to treat them as separate words anymore. Compare the same mixture of roots in muffelig.|Pronunciation}IPA:/ˈmʊfɪç/qualifier:standard}IPA:/ˈmʊfɪk/qualifier:common form in southern Germany,Austria,and Switzerland}Ⓓb/b4/De-muffig.ogg}muf+fig|Adjective}#generally smelly,stinking,particularly:having a moldy smell}#of a room,furniture uninviting,fusty,in need of renovation}#of a person grumpy,unfriendly}#figurative old-fashioned,reactionary

*Muttern*de{}|Pronunciation}IPA:ˈmʊtɐn}Ⓓ6/61/De-Muttern.ogg|Noun}Muttern:}#Form of [Mutter]|Noun}Muttern:}#archaic Form of [Mutter]|Usage notes}The dialectal inflected form '''''Muttern''''' is (or was) applied in the dative and accusative cases when used without an article,i.e. in the sense of “mum”:''Du sollst Mutter'''n''' helfen.'' — “You're supposed to help Mum.” This was typical of eastern German dialects,including that of Berlin,but is now widely obsolete. A remnant of this is the phrase wie bei Muttern,which is in general use.
